title: Derived CuSn Alloys from Heterointerfaces in Bimetallic Oxides Promote the CO2 Electroreduction to Formate
abstract: Electroreduction of CO2 into valuable chemicals provides a promising strategy for mitigating excessive CO2 emissions and storing intermittent renewable energy. Herein, SnO2/CuOnanoparticle composites (NCs) with rich heterointerfaces were designed for selectively converting CO2 into liquidus formate. Distinct from only monometallic phase evolved in physicallymixed samples, Cu and Sn atoms at the heterointerfaces were in-situ reduced into alloys under working conditions. With residual SnOx/CuOx stabilizing the CO2 * intermediate, CuSn alloys can obviously suppress the undesired hydrogen evolution reaction and then enhance the catalytic selectivity. In a H-type cell, as-obtained SnO2/CuO NCs exhibit Faraday efficiency (FE) of 89.3% and current density of 18.34 mAcm 2 for formate, which is stable for 30 h at 1.0 V vs. RHE. Impressively, the formate current density of 310 mAcm 2 is achieved in a flow cell. Moreover, constructing efficient samples by the heterointerfaces engineering would provide an inspiration for designing novel electrocatalysts.

sections.text:

Electroreduction of CO2 into valuable chemicals provides a promising strategy for mitigating excessive CO2 emissions and storing intermittent renewable energy. Herein, SnO2/CuOnanoparticle composites (NCs) with rich heterointerfaces were designed for selectively converting CO2 into liquidus formate. Distinct from only monometallic phase evolved in physicallymixed samples, Cu and Sn atoms at the heterointerfaces were in-situ reduced into alloys under working conditions. With residual SnOx/CuOx stabilizing the CO2 * intermediate, CuSn alloys can obviously suppress the undesired hydrogen evolution reaction and then enhance the catalytic selectivity. In a H-type cell, as-obtained SnO2/CuO NCs exhibit Faraday efficiency (FE) of 89.3% and current density of 18.34 mAcm 2 for formate, which is stable for 30 h at 1.0 V vs. RHE. Impressively, the formate current density of 310 mAcm 2 is achieved in a flow cell. Moreover, constructing efficient samples by the heterointerfaces engineering would provide an inspiration for designing novel electrocatalysts.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) towards fuels or chemicals is promising for renewable energy storage and mitigating the global climate crisis caused by excessive CO2 emissions.[1–3] Among the products (such as CO, CH4, formate and other hydrocarbons) in CO2RR, formate is an important chemical intermediate and potential hydrogen carrier, which is also effortless to be transported and stored.[4–6] Compared with precious metals (Pd) and toxic metals (Pb, Cd, Hg), Sn-based and Cu-based materials have become the research hotspot for generating formate due to their low cost, high abundance and eco-friendliness.[7–10] Nevertheless, simplex metal materials usually exhibit low electrocatalytic activity and selectivity for formate because of the formation of H2 and other CO2RR products. For example, tin oxide or copper oxide with appropriate orbital energy and electron configurations presents relatively poor catalytic activity owing to their poor conductivity.[11] Therefore, it is of great practical significance to develop efficient Sn and Cu oxide CO2RR electrocatalysts with high FE for producing formate.
Up to now, it is a feasible remedy to improve CO2RR performance of metallic oxide electrocatalysts by combining with the highly conductive zero-valance metal.[12,13] Taking as an
example, Jiao et al. constructed core-shell Ag Sn catalysts with a highly conductive Ag Sn core and SnO2 shell about 1.7 nm thick, which can achieve desirable current density (j= 16 mAcm 2) with high FE of 80%.[14] Under CO2 electroreduction condition, simplex metal oxide electrocatalysts can partially insitu convert to metallic phase that can directly combine adjacent residual metal oxides to form the metal/metal oxides active phase.[15–17] However, with the increase of a single zero valent metal, the formation of H2 will be accelerated, resulting in a diminished CO2RR selectivity.
[18] It has been reported that alloy could efficiently adjust the selectivity of CO2RR compared with a single metal.[19] For example, Cui et al. prepared CuSn alloy by co-electrodeposition, which restrain the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and CO production, thus improving the selectivity of formate.[20] However, the in-situ formation of bimetallic alloys under CO2 electroreduction condition is still a huge challenge, because it requires the close contact of two metals at the atomic level. Thereby, reasonable constructing Cu Sn oxide electrocatalysts which Cu and Sn atoms can partially in-situ alloy under CO2 reduction condition would be a feasible strategy for enhancing their performance in

sections.heading: CO2RR.
sections.text:
This work constructs the SnO2/CuO NCs which can further in-situ convert into efficient active site of CuSn alloy by heterointerfaces engineering during CO2RR process. In a typical H-type cell with CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution, the optimal SnO2/CuO NCs deliver FEformate of 89.3% with formate partial current density of 18.34 mAcm 2 and long-term stability for 30 h at 1.0 V vs. RHE. Furthermore, it can even exhibit an ultrahigh formate current density of 310 mAcm 2 at 0.63 V vs. RHE in a flow cell, indicating its potential application possibility. Based on the investigation of active components under CO2RR condition, the excellent performance originates from the synergistic effect of diversified active sites derived from the SnO2/CuO NCs during CO2RR process. sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
In this work, the SnO2/CuO NCs are synthesized by coprecipitation and subsequent thermal annealing. As shown in Figure 1a and S1, the SnO2/CuO NCs are composed by connected nanoparticles with diameters around 8 nm. The corresponding selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern can be effortless indexed to the crystal planes of the SnO2 and CuO without other impurity. In the high resolution TEM (HRTEM) image (Figure 1b), the clear fringe spacings of 0.33 and 0.25 nm assigned to SnO2 (110) and CuO (002) facet, respectively, which shows obvious interface. This result demonstrates the SnO2/CuO heterointerfaces have formed in the SnO2/CuO NCs. The elemental distributions of the SnO2/CuO NCs are shown in Figure S2, where the Sn, Cu, O elements are homogeneously distributed in the whole structure. The typical SEM image in Figure S3 shows the SnO2/CuO NCs are fluffy structures assembled from ultrafine nanoparticles, which can expose more electrochemical active sites. Meanwhile, the SEM image (Figure S4b, c) shows that the SnO2/CuO-1 NCs (high content SnO2) and the SnO2/CuO-2 NCs (low content SnO2) as the comparison samples of optimizing the electrochemical performance have similar structure to the SnO2/CuO NCs. Furthermore, the microstructure of the SnO2 and the CuO
nanoparticles are exhibited in (Figure S5 and Figure S6). The grain size of the SnO2 and the CuO is larger than that of the SnO2/CuO NCs, indicating that bimetallic co-precipitation can effectively inhibit the growth of nanoparticles compared to single-metal precipitation.[21]
The corresponding XRD patterns of the SnO2/CuO NCs, the SnO2 CuO physical mixture, the SnO2, and the CuO are shown in Figure 1c. It can be found that all diffraction peaks can be assigned to the SnO2 (JCPDS: 41-1445) and the CuO (JCPDS: 45- 0937) phases, in accordance with the SAED result. According to inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry (ICPAES) result (Table. S1), the atomic ratio of CuO and SnO2 in the SnO2/CuO NCs is around 0.72 :1. The bonding form of the SnO2/ CuO NCs is characterized by Raman spectroscopy (Figure 1d), where two distinct peaks at 270 cm 1 and 498 cm 1 correspond to the characteristic peaks of the Cu O bond in CuO and the Sn O bond in SnO2, respectively.
[22,23] It should be noted that one large peak at 615 cm 1 may be assigned to the accumulative peak of Cu O and Sn O. Moreover, the chemical composition and surface chemical state of the catalysts were identified by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The clear Sn, Cu, and O peaks appear in the XPS survey spectra of the SnO2/CuO NCs (Figure S7). The Sn 3d region (Figure 1e) can be deconvoluted into two characteristic peaks located at 486.4 and 494.8 eV, corresponding to Sn4+.[24] Specially, Sn species in the SnO2/CuO NCs are slightly smaller than those for the SnO2 and the SnO2 CuO physical mixture, indicating that more electrons transfer to the SnO2 from CuO benefiting from the formation of heterointerface. In addition, Cu 2p3/2 peak in the SnO2/CuO NCs shows higher binding energy than the other two samples (Figure 1f), which further demonstrate the above result. Moreover, the presence of the shakeup peak at 941.2 eV and 943.8 eV suggests the existence of Cu2+.[25] Therefore, the above results manifest the strong electronic interaction between SnO2 and CuO in theSnO2/CuO NCs, further confirming the construction of the SnO2/CuO heterointerfaces. Figure S8 displays the UPS spectra and derived work functions of the SnO2/CuO NCs, the SnO2 CuO physical mixture, the SnO2, and the CuO. Obviously, the SnO2/CuO NCs have the lowest work function among the four samples, contributing to faster electron transfer, which consequently results in the improvement of CO2RR activity.[26] Based on the above results, it is concluded that the prepared SnO2/CuO NCs have rich SnO2/CuO heterointerfaces, which ensures that abundant Cu atoms are in close contact with Sn atoms at the atomic scale and promote CuSn alloy formation under CO2RR reduction condition.
The CO2RR performances of the metal oxide catalysts were carried out in a typical H-type cell filled with CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution. Figure 2a and Figure S9 compare the FE and partial current density of the electrocatalysts for generating formate at 1.0 and 0.8 V vs. RHE. It can be found that the SnO2/CuO NCs possess the optimal catalytic performance. To investigate the possible influence of the SnO2/CuO heterointerfaces on catalytic properties, we further compared the SnO2/ CuO NCs with the pure SnO2, the CuO and the SnO2 CuO physical mixture electrocatalysts for CO2RR in similar conditions. Furthermore, the gaseous and liquid products obtained during CO2RR were quantified by online gas chromatography and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analyses, respectively (Figure S11).[27]
The FE of the major electrocatalytic products (formate, CO and H2) at different potentials are compared in Figure 2b and Figure S12. Dramatically, theSnO2/CuO NCs show the highest formate selectivity at a relatively low potential ranging from
0.8 to 1.0 V vs. RHE, compared with the SnO2, the CuO and the SnO2 CuO physical mixture. Specifically, the FEformate of the SnO2/CuO NCs reaches 83.1% (61.3% for the SnO2, 23.8% for the CuO and 44.1% for the SnO2 CuO physical mixture) at 0.8 V vs. RHE. At the same time, the generation of H2 is also effectively suppressed in the SnO2/CuO NCs. As shown in Figure 2c, the jformate of the SnO2/CuO NCs was higher than that of other samples at all applied potentials. Especially, when the applied potential was set at 1.0 V vs. RHE, the SnO2/CuO NCs achieve a maximum FE of 89.3% for formate production, and its jformate reaches 18.34 mAcm
2. In addition, the SnO2/CuO NCs also exhibit prominent stability. It can constantly provide a formate current density of about 19.0 mAcm 2 for 30 h, as well as the excellent FEformate (� 81.6%) at 1.0 V vs. RHE (Figure 2d). This performance indicates that the SnO2/CuO NCs also exhibit the superior FE and the current density for formate among the reported Sn or Cu based catalysts (Table S2). The above electrochemical results indicate that the SnO2/CuO heterointerfaces in the SnO2/CuO NCs have a remarkably positive effect on the electrocatalytic activity of CO2-to-formate.
To gain the structural information of the obtained active sites under CO2RR conditions, the composition and morphology of the SnO2/CuO NCs and the SnO2 CuO physical mixture without SnO2/CuO heterointerfaces were further characterized after CO2RR. As shown in Figure 3a, at 15 min-CO2RR at 1.0 V vs. RHE, weak CuSn alloy diffraction peaks already appear in the SnO2/CuO NCs electrocatalysts, while the peaks of SnO2 and CuO completely disappeared. After 30 min-CO2RR, the diffraction peaks of the catalyst do not change obviously. This results show that the partial reconstruction of the SnO2/CuO NCs toward CuSn alloy is very fast. TEM and SEM images (Figure 3b and S13-14) of the 30 min-SnO2/ CuO NCs and the 12 h-SnO2/CuO NCs after CO2RR exhibit a similar nanoparticle morphology with diameters around 30 nm. The HRTEM image (Figure 3c) shows a planar spacing of 0.29 nm related to (101) facet of CuSn alloy. No obvious lattice fringe near CuSn alloy in nanoparticles is observed, indicating the existence of amorphous metastable metal oxides.[28] EDS mappings (Figure S15) reveal that Sn, Cu, O atoms are homogeneously distributed in whole electrocatalysts. In the high-resolution Sn 3d XPSspectra (Figure 3d) of the SnO2/CuO NCs and the SnO2 CuO physical mixture after 30 min or 12 hCO2RR, two weak peaks centered at 485.1 and 493.5 eV are identified as Sn0, meanwhile a large amount of oxidized tin could be observed.[29] In the Figure 3e, the Auger electron spectroscopy of Cu LMM signal clearly shows that both the SnO2/CuO NCs catalysts and the SnO2 CuO physical mixture after 30 min and 12 h-CO2RR possess metallic Cu
0 (568.0 eV). Due to the different Cu O bonds in the residual CuOx after CO2RR, the binding energy of oxidized Cu
+ (569.4 eV) in the SnO2/CuO NCs catalysts is different from that (569.9 eV) of the SnO2 CuO physical mixture, consistent with the Cu 2p3/2 XPS spectra in Figure S16.[30] The above results confirm that the SnO2/CuO NCs catalysts will be fast in-situ converted into diversified efficient active sites containing CuSn alloy and residual SnOx/CuOx due to the engineering of the rich SnO2/ CuO heterointerfaces, while the SnO2 CuO physical mixture without heterointerface only forms a mixture of metal Sn with SnOx and metal Cu with CuOx during CO2RR. The enhanced performance of the SnO2/CuO NCs is further illustrated in Figure 3f. The residual metastable SnOx/CuOx in the SnO2/CuO NCs significantly enhances the CO2RR performance by strengthening the CO2 adsorption and stabilizing reduced CO2 intermediates (CO2
* ).[31,32] What’s more, CuSn alloy could suppress HER activity more effectively than single metal Cu and Sn derived from the SnO2 CuO physical mixture during CO2RR, thereby enhancing formate selectivityand catalytic activity.[33]
To deeply evaluate the kinetics of formate formation, the Tafel plots of the formate partial currents were investigated and presented in Figure 4a. The SnO2/CuO NCs deliver the smallest value of 123.4 mVdec 1 in comparison to the SnO2 CuO physical mixture (163.9 mVdec 1), the SnO2 (170.7 mVdec
1) and the CuO (197.7 mVdec 1) electrocatalysts, confirming the improved kinetics toward formate due to the generation of more efficient CuSn phase. Notably, the Tafel slope of the SnO2/ CuO NCs is very close to the theoretical value of 118 mVdec 1, indicating that its rate-limiting step is the activation of CO2.
[34] In Figure 4b, the interfacial charge transfer resistance (Rct) of the SnO2/CuO NCs, the SnO2 CuO physical mixture, the SnO2 and the CuO is 26.3, 30.1, 36.9 and 4.3 Ω, respectively. Such results reveal the SnO2/CuO NCs have faster dynamics than the SnO2 CuO physical mixture and SnO2, except for CuO that has facilitate HER rather than CO2RR.
[35] Of note, the first electron transfer step (the adsorbed CO2 +e !CO2 * ) is the rate-limiting step, in which stabilization of the CO2 * intermediate plays a significant role in CO2RR to formate. To verify the binding
affinity of CO2 * on samples, adsorption of OH as a surrogate was carried out by oxidative LSV scans at 100 mVs 1 in Arbubbled 0.1 M NaOH electrolyte.[36] And, the potential for surface OH adsorption on SnO2/CuO NCs is the most negative, indicating strongest adsorption affinity of OH . sections.heading: 3. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, the SnO2/CuO NCs with rich heterointerfaces were synthesized and presented superior electrocatalytic abilities for reducing CO2 into liquidus formate. In a typical H-type cell, the SnO2/CuO NCs exhibit FE of 89.3% and partial current density of 18.34 mAcm 2 for formate, as well as impressive stability for 30 h at 1.0 V vs. RHE in 0.5 M CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution. Moreover, the formate current density of 310 mAcm 2 at 0.63 V vs. RHE is achieved in a flow cell reactor, indicating the feasibility of practical application for as-obtained catalysts. Detailed characterization results ascribed the enhanced catalytic performance to synergistic effects, while the residual SnOx/CuOx could stabilize the CO2
* intermediate of CO2 reduction and the CuSn alloys suppress the undesired hydrogen evolution. Distinct from only monometallic phase evolved in physicallymixed samples, Cu and Sn atoms at heterointerfaces were insitu reduced into alloys under CO2RR conditions. This constructing strategy through heterointerface engineering under working conditions would provide a guidance for preparing novel efficient electrocatalysts.

sections.heading: Electrocatalysts synthesis
sections.text: SnO2/CuO NCs electrocatalysts with rich heterointerfaces were prepared by co-precipitation and subsequent calcination methods. In a typical process, the total molar amount of metal ions is 5 mmol. CuCl2 and SnCl2 with a certain molar ratio (seeing Table S1 for details) were added into 50 mL of deionized water to obtain a homogeneous emulsion solution under continuous stirring for 1 h. Then concentrated ammonia hydroxide was added dropwise to the above solution until neutral. After vigorously stirring for another 2 h, the resultant precipitate was centrifugated, washed with deionized water and ethanol, and then dried overnight in a vacuum oven at 80 °C. Afterwards, the precipitate was annealed at 400 °C for 2 h in a muffle furnace. Finally, a series of SnO2/CuO NCs were obtained after naturally cooling to room temperature. As comparisons, the pure SnO2 and CuO were also synthesized by the similar method. In addition, the SnO2 CuO physical mixture was obtained by grinding the pure SnO2 and CuO in an agate mortar for 30 minutes.

sections.heading: Materials characterizations
sections.text:
The crystal structure of the electrocatalysts was determined by X ray diffraction (XRD; Rigaku D/Max 2550, Cu Ka radiation). The morphology of the samples was characterized by field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, Hitachi, S-4800, 10 kV) and field emission transmission electron microscopy (FETEM, JEOL, JEM-
2100 F) with an X-ray energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). The chemical states of the electrocatalysts were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi). The ultraviolet photoemission spectroscopy (UPS) was measured with a Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi and a VG Scienta R4000 analyzer (monochromatic He I light source of 21.2 eV). Raman measurement was carried out by using a spectrometer (Via+Reflex) at an excitation wavelength of 532 nm. CO2 adsorption isotherms were performed by using a Quantachrome Autosorb-IQ-MP apparatus at 25 °C.

sections.heading: Electrochemical measurements
sections.text: The 5 mg of catalyst was dispersed in the mixture of 1 mL of ethanol and 20 μL of Nafion solution (5 wt%) by ultrasound for 1 h. Then, 200 μL of catalyst ink was uniformly dropped onto a carbon fiber paper (1×1 cm 2) to prepare working electrode with an areal loading of 1 mg cm 2. Most electrochemical experiments were performed on a Chi660E potentiostat (CHI Instrument) in a Nafion membrane separated H-type cell. Pt mesh, Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) and CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution (0.5 M, pH is about 7.2) were served as the counter electrode, the reference electrode and electrolyte, respectively. The flow rate of CO2 into the catholyte was 5 sccm min 1 during electrolysis. All the tested potentials were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) without special statement in this work. All electrochemical results were measured without IR-compensated. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves were obtained at 10 mVs 1. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was recorded at 1.0 V vs. RHE with the frequency ranging from 0.1 Hz to 105 Hz at a sinusoidal voltage amplitude of 5 mV on an Autolab potentiostat (AUT85315). CV measurements at various scan rates were performed to obtain the double layer capacitance (Cdl) that is proportional to the electrochemical active area.

sections.heading: Flow cell measurements
sections.text:
Flow cell measurements were conducted in a flow cell reactor. The SnO2/CuO NCs loaded gas diffusion electrodes (GDL, 1 mgcm
2, 2× 3 cm2), platinum sheet and saturated Ag/AgCl electrode were used as the working, counter, and reference electrodes, respectively. The electrolyte was 1 M KOH. During the measurements, CO2 gas was directly supported to the working electrode at a rate of 15 sccm. All electrochemical data were obtained in Flow cell reactor with 75%- IR-compensated.

sections.heading: Products analysis
sections.text: All the gas products were quantified via an on-line gas chromatography (GC2060, Ramiin), equipped with flame ionization detector (FID) and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). Ar (99.999%) was used as carrier gas. Liquid products were analyzed by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, 600 MHz) spectroscopy. Typically, the measured sample was made by mixing the 0.5 mL of collected catholyte and 0.1 mL of D2O solution (with TMSP used as internal standard). The 1H spectra were collected by using a pre-saturation method for water suppression.
